and wrote five factual claims about those records. Now we will use our new tools and methods to dig deeper into the data. Specifically, we will now be able to ask "which one" and "top ten" questions. Every one of
the tasks below uses these new patterns. 

Work in **pairs**, in one shared notebook, taking turns at the keyboard. Swap every time you
finish a numbered task. The person not typing should read through the output (quietly) and explain what the code should produce/calculate before you run it. 

We have about 45 minutes for this activity. Please tell Cella or Kelly if you get stuck,

## The data

The same file you explored yesterday:

```
https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/national_parks.csv
```

Two things you saw yesterday will matter today:

- the `year` column is stored as **text**, not as numbers
- some rows have a `year` of `Total` rather than an actual year

## Setup

Create a notebook named `Colab_3D_Ranking_Questions.ipynb`, with both partners' names in the
title cell, then read the file in and check its shape.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/national_parks.csv'
parks = pd.read_csv(url)
parks.shape
```

parks.columns.tolist()

## Our two new patterns

You have both of these in your session notebooks already, the filter pattern from this morning
and the top-N pattern from earlier this afternoon, but here they are as a reminder:

```python
df[df['column'] > value]                                # the filter pattern
df.sort_values('column', ascending=False).head(n)       # the top-N pattern
```

## Part 1: Filtering (about 15 minutes)

Answer each question with code, then write the answer in a markdown cell underneath, in a
complete sentence with the number in it.

1. How many rows describe units whose `unit_type` is exactly `National Park`?

```{python}
national_parks = parks[parks['unit_type'] == 'National Park']
national_parks.shape
```

2. How many rows have a `year` of `Total`? Use `~` or `!=` to build a table called
   `by_year` that has none of them in it. How many rows does `by_year` have?

```{python}
totals = parks[parks['year'] == 'Total']
print(totals.shape)

by_year = parks[~(parks['year'] == 'Total')]
print(by_year.shape)
```

3. The `region` column uses two-letter codes. Build a **list** of the codes `PW`, `IM`, and
   `AK`, and use `.isin()` to filter `by_year` down to units in those three regions. How many
   rows?

```{python}
western_regions = ['PW', 'IM', 'AK']
western = by_year[by_year['region'].isin(western_regions)]
western.shape
```

4. Using two conditions in one filter, find the rows that are National Parks **and** recorded
   more than 5 million visitors. How many are there, and what does each row represent?

```{python}
big = by_year[(by_year['unit_type'] == 'National Park') & (by_year['visitors'] > 5_000_000)]
print(big.shape)
big[['year', 'unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']].sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head()
```

:::{.callout-tip title="Stuck on the parentheses?"}
Every comparison inside a combined filter needs its own set of parentheses:
`(a == b) & (c > d)`. If you get a `TypeError` that mentions something you did not write,
missing parentheses are almost always the reason.
:::

## Part 2: Ranking (about 15 minutes)

5. Rank **all** of `parks` by `visitors`, largest first, and look at the top 10. Something is
   wrong with this answer. Say what, and say why in one sentence.

```{python}
parks.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[
    ['year', 'unit_name', 'unit_type', 'visitors']
]
```

6. Fix it, and rank `by_year` instead. Which single park unit had the highest visitor count in
   any one year, and in what year?

```{python}
by_year.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[
    ['year', 'unit_name', 'unit_type', 'state', 'visitors']
]
```

7. Filter to National Parks in the year `2016`, then find the top 10 by visitors. Show only
   the `unit_name`, `state`, and `visitors` columns.

```{python}
np_2016 = by_year[(by_year['unit_type'] == 'National Park') & (by_year['year'] == '2016')].copy()
print(np_2016.shape)

np_2016.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[['unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']]
```

8. How many of the 61 National Parks recorded more than a million visitors in 2016?

```{python}
(np_2016['visitors'] > 1_000_000).sum()
```

9. Use `.idxmax()` and `.loc[]` on `np_2016` to print the name of the most-visited National
   Park of 2016 on its own, without displaying the whole row.

```{python}
busiest = np_2016['visitors'].idxmax()
print(np_2016.loc[busiest, 'unit_name'])
print(np_2016.loc[busiest, 'visitors'])
```

## Part 3: Put them together (about 10 minutes)

10. Build a list of the state codes `CA`, `UT`, and `AZ`. Filter `np_2016` to National Parks
    in those three states, rank them by visitors, and display the whole ranked list.

```{python}
southwest_states = ['CA', 'UT', 'AZ']
southwest = np_2016[np_2016['state'].isin(southwest_states)].copy()

southwest.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False)[['unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']]
```

11. Which of those three states has the park at the top of your list, and which has the most
    parks in it? Answer both in a markdown cell. You can count the parks per state by eye from
    your ranked table.

```{python}
southwest['state'].value_counts()
```

12. In one markdown cell of three or four sentences, answer this: **a colleague asks you which
    national park is "the busiest". What do you need to know before you can answer, and what
    would you tell them?** Use at least two numbers from today's work.

:::{.callout-note title="If you finish early"}
Pick a year other than 2016 and produce the same top 10. Did the order change? Name one park
that moved several places, if any of them did, and say what you would need in order to find
out whether that movement is real or an artifact of how the data was recorded.

Do not try to compare all the years at once. That needs grouping, and we get to grouping later this week.
:::
